lessons.title: Greedy algorithms
lessons.summary: Make the best local choice at each step, and learn when that is provably optimal.

slides.title: What is greedy?
slides.text:
A **greedy** algorithm makes the choice that looks **best right now** and never goes back.

- Simple and fast (often just a sort + one pass)
- Correct **only for some problems**: you must argue why
slides.narration: A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, always taking the choice that looks best right now and never reconsidering. Greedy solutions are usually short and fast, often just a sort followed by one pass. The catch is that greedy is only correct for some problems, so you must be able to explain why it works.

slides.title: Activity selection
slides.text:
Given meetings `[start, end)`, choose the **most** that do not overlap.

Greedy rule: **sort by end time**, take a meeting if it starts at or after the last chosen end.
slides.code:
meetings = [(1, 4), (3, 5), (0, 6), (5, 7), (8, 9), (5, 9)]
meetings.sort(key=lambda m: m[1])
count, last_end = 0, float("-inf")
for s, e in meetings:
    if s >= last_end:
        count += 1
        last_end = e
print(count)   # 3: (1,4), (5,7), (8,9)
slides.narration: The classic greedy problem is scheduling the most meetings in one room. Sort the meetings by their end time. Then walk through them and take each meeting that starts no earlier than the end of the last one you took. Finishing early leaves the most room for everything else.

slides.title: Why earliest end works
slides.text:
**Exchange argument**: take any optimal schedule. Swap its first meeting for the one that **ends earliest**. It still fits (it ends no later), so the count is unchanged.

Repeat for the rest: greedy is optimal.
slides.narration: Why is this correct? Use an exchange argument. Take any best schedule and replace its first meeting with the meeting that ends earliest overall. Because it ends no later, nothing else conflicts, and the number of meetings stays the same. Repeating this step by step turns any optimal schedule into the greedy one.

slides.title: When greedy fails
slides.text:
- Coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6: greedy gives 4+1+1, best is 3+3
- 0/1 knapsack: highest value first can be wrong
- Shortest paths with negative edges

If you cannot prove it, **test it** against brute force on small inputs.
slides.narration: Greedy is often wrong. With coins one, three and four, taking the biggest coin first gives three coins for six, while two coins are enough. Picking the most valuable items first fails for the zero one knapsack. A good habit is to compare your greedy solution with a brute force solution on many small random inputs.

slides.title: Famous greedy algorithms
slides.text:
- **Huffman coding** (compression)
- **Kruskal / Prim**: minimum spanning tree
- **Dijkstra** (greedy choice of closest vertex)
- Fractional knapsack: best value per weight
- Scheduling by deadline / end time
slides.narration: Many famous algorithms are greedy. Huffman coding merges the two rarest symbols first. Kruskal and Prim build minimum spanning trees by adding the cheapest safe edge. Dijkstra greedily finalizes the closest vertex. And the fractional knapsack, where you can take parts of items, is solved by taking the best value per kilogram first.

lessons.notes:
## Greedy recipe

1. Find a **rule** that picks the next piece of the answer (often after sorting).
2. **Prove** it: an exchange argument or "greedy stays ahead".
3. Implement: usually O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n).

## Activity selection (interval scheduling)

```python
intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])   # by end time
count, last = 0, -inf
for s, e in intervals:
    if s >= last:        # touching is allowed for [s, e)
        count += 1; last = e
```

Sorting by **start** time or by **length** does not work:
- by start: `(0, 100)` would block many short meetings.
- by length: a short meeting in the middle can block two longer ones.

## Exchange argument

Show that any optimal solution can be changed, step by step, into the greedy solution without getting worse. Then greedy is optimal too.

## Classic greedy problems

| Problem | Greedy choice |
|---|---|
| Interval scheduling | earliest end time |
| Minimum platforms / rooms | sort events, sweep |
| Fractional knapsack | highest value/weight ratio |
| Huffman coding | merge two least frequent |
| Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal) | cheapest edge without a cycle |
| Coin change with 1, 2, 5, 10, ... | largest coin first (works for canonical coin systems only) |

## Greedy vs DP

Greedy commits to one choice; DP considers all choices for each subproblem. If greedy has a counterexample, DP is often the fix (like coin change). Greedy is faster and simpler when it is correct.

## Testing tip

Write a brute force (try all subsets for n <= 10), generate random tests, and compare. Any difference is a counterexample.
